Currently (0.5-9), lavaan only has the WLS(MV) estimator available for
ordinal data, so we can not use FIML. I would not recommend single
imputation. You could use multiple imputation, using for example the
'mice' package (probably Amelia too). Once you have those imputed
datasets, you need to run the model on each of them, and aggregate the
results using Rubin's rules. In the semTools package, there is a runMI()
function that does this automatically for continuous data. It is
probably not too hard to adapt this for ordinal data... (and that is why
I have Alex in cc).

Yves.

Hi all,

The topic of incorporating ordinal data analysis into the runMI function has been kicked around here over the last week or two. Currently, I believe that runMI can work for ordinal data with a couple of caveats.

1. We have not explicitly tested runMI with ordinal data, so I won't promise that it will work. With that said, I'm fairly sure that runMI should be able to combine parameter estimates and standard errors in a model with ordinal data.
2. The issue with using runMI with ordinal data is computing model fit information. Currently we haven't updated runMI to incorporate the fit indices related to ordinal data. This is especially relevant for the Mplus and Meng & Rubin chi square statistics. I believe that if you request the Li, Meng, Raghunathan & Rubin chi square statistics (set chi= 'LMRR' in runMI), your models will run.

If you decide to test this out, please let me know, I'd be very curious to hear about your experience using runMI with ordinal data and any suggestions you have.

Thanks,

-Alex

Your dataset contains unordered factors (categorical variables). [which
is weird, if they are just numeric values 1,2,3,4,5; I would check the
input file; perhaps all the numbers are quoted? In that case, remove the
quotes; OR, did you forget 'header=TRUE' in the call to read.table to
get the variable names?]

To treat them as ordinal variables, you need to declare them as
'ordered'. You can do this before you call lavaan as follows:

Data[,] <- lapply(Data[,], ordered)

(here I assume *all* variables are ordered; if only a selection is
ordinal, while others are continuous, use something like:

Data[,c("item1","item2","item3","item4")] <-
lapply(Data[,c("item1","item2","item3","item4")], ordered)

If you now call the cfa() function, lavaan will treat the 'ordered'
variables as ordinal.

Another approach is to leave the data as it is, and to declare variables
as ordered usin the 'ordered' argument in the cfa() call:

fit<-cfa(AE.model, data=study1, ordered=c("V1","V2","V3",....) )

The latter approach has the advantage that you can switch between a
continuous approach and an ordinal approach to deal with likert scale items.

Hope this helps,

Yves.

That would be *single* imputation. And although that is ok for getting
parameter estimates only, you can not trust the standard errors (or the
test statistic). For that, you need *multiple* imputations. So you do
this multiple times (say, 10 times), and then you need to aggregate the
results. How to do the latter is what the runMI() function does in the
semTools package.

I don't believe that lavaan will automatically include auxiliary variables. However, the auxiliary function in semTools will definitely do the job. The code to use auxiliary in your case should be pretty straight forward:

auxvars = c("NALTREXO","GENDER","AGE","DEPNDSX","T0_PHD")

model1 = 'T4_PHD ~ 1 + THERAPY'

fit.fiml = sem(model1, data=raw.dataset, estimator="ML", missing="FIML")
fit.aux <- auxiliary(fit.fiml, aux = auxvars, data=raw.dataset, estimator="ML", missing="FIML")
summary(fit.aux)

There are a couple of situations where the auxiliary function runs into trouble, and a simple regrression like this might be one. If you run into trouble, you might also think about using multiple imputations in lieu of FIML and auxiliary variables.

-Alex

> use "all available data" to help give the best estimate for missing
> values (i.e., they are auxiliary), or if that just meant it doesn't use

I agree this is not very clear indeed. But lavaan does NOT use auxiliary
variables. It only uses the (observed) variables that are included in
your model.

However -just to see if it makes a difference- you can easily trick
lavaan to use auxiliary variables: you add them to the model, but you
make sure they have no effect, for example:

model1 = 'T4_PHD ~ 1 + THERAPY + 0*NALTREXO + 0*THERAPY'

Here, both NALTREXO and THERAPY will be used as auxiliary variables.
Note, however, that we assume that all these variables are continuous;
we assume multivariate normality (and I'm not sure about THERAPY, but
GENDER should not be included!). Another caveat is that the degrees of
freedom will be off, but you can get them from the original analysis.

The same is true for the auxiliary() in semTools: only use continuous
variables!

> My code is a simple regression model:
>
> auxvars =
> c("NALTREXO","THERAPY","GENDER","AGE","DEPNDSX","T0_PHD","T4_PHD")
> model1 = 'T4_PHD ~ 1 + THERAPY'
> fit.fiml = sem(model1, data=raw.dataset[,auxvars], estimator="ML",
> missing="FIML")
> summary(fit.fiml)
>
> Although only the T4_PHD and THERAPY variables are used in the model, I
> would like the 5 additional auxiliary variables to help give the most
> accurate estimate of the model given missing data for T4_PHD.

In my understanding, auxiliary variables are not used when estimating
the model parameters! They are only used to fit the unrestricted (h1)
model (ie. the covariance matrix of the incomplete data). The latter is
only needed to compute the model test statistic. Your estimates (and
standard errors) will be fine without them.

Yves.

I want to test a model where the constraint on one parameters is defined by the fraction of two other parameters.

On 10/18/2012 10:54 AM, Dr. Hans Hansen wrote:
> Dear lavaan users,
>
> as far as i understand regression models are a special case of the more
> general structural equation models. i wonder, whether it is possible to
> model logistic regression in lavaan? Wouldn't one just need to transform
> the left-hand-side of the formula with the logit? Probably it's much
> more complicated, isn't it?

It is. Lavaan can not handle logistic regression (yet). It can handle
probit regression (using the probit link instead of the logit link) for
binary outcomes. But parameters can only be estimated by using WLS(MV),
not ML (at least not in 0.5-9), but the results are typically almost
identical. The only downside is that you can not directly interpret the
(exponentiated) regression coefficients as odds (ratios).

This would be an example (if y is binary):

model <- ' y ~ x1 + x2 + x3'
fit <- sem(model, data=myData, ordered="y")

Yves.

> I have a series of univariate growth curve analyses to do, with models like:

>   s.panas_pos =~0*panas_pos.1+1*panas_pos.2+2*panas_pos.3+3*panas_pos.4
> # regressions
>   i.panas_pos ~ age0 +grp

> |

> run ï¿½growth(mymod,mydf)ï¿½ in that case, I get a warning that grp is not
> ordered.

Indeed. This is a reminder that lavaan syntax (unlike, say, lm formulas)
does (currently) NOT automatically expand nominal factors to a set of
dummy variables. You should take care of that yourself. If you have two
levels, you just need a (numeric) binary variable with two values (say 1
and 0). As long as it is an exogenous (independent) variable, there is
no need to treat it special.

If I precede growth() with

>    mydf$grp<-ordered(mydf$grp)
> |
>
> then I get an error:
> |
> Errorinsamplestats@cov[[g]][cbind(row.idx,col.idx)]:
>    subscript outof bounds

That is because lavaan can not handle 'ordered' exogenous variables (and
your group variable is not ordered; it is just nominal). On the other
hand, lavaan could catch this, convert it back to numeric, and proceed
as usual. I'll fix this in the dev version. (But in the meantime, do not
'order' exogenous variables).

is not positive-definite (ie not of full rank). Therefore, it can not be
inverted.

others? You need to get rid of these redundant predictors first, to get
an 'X' matrix which is of full rank.

Before you do your analysis, you can use

qr(X)$rank

to check the rank of the matrix X.

Alternately, if it is a recursive SEM with only observed variables, you should be able to take simulated draws of the coefficients and errors to get predictions with 95% CIs on them.  It will just take some doing on your part.

Here's a simple example - although it does make me wonder if, for a case like this, this could be automated…

Sorry, haven't dug into lavaan's guts lately to come up with a classier more elegant solution for this one.

library(lavaan)

#create a data frame
set.seed(1001)
n <- 100
adf <- data.frame(x1 = rnorm(n))
adf <- within(adf, {
  x2 <- rnorm(n)
  y1 <- rnorm(n, x1 + x2)
  y2 <- rnorm(n, y1 + x2)
})

#create a fit sem object
model <- '
  y1 ~ x1 + x2
  y2 ~ y1 + x2
'
fit <- sem(model, data = adf)

#now, use simulation to determine
#a new y2 value based on x1 and x2
n.sims <- 100
new.x <- c(1,2)

#get the coefficients
coefs <- rmvnorm(n.sims, coef(fit), vcov(fit))

#get the residual SE for each response variable
#using the inverse chisq distribution
df <- nrow(adf)-1
X <- matrix(rchisq(n.sims*2, df=df), ncol=2)
ses <- sqrt( coef(fit)[5:6]) * sqrt(df/X)

#calculate the new y1 and y3
y1.pred <- rnorm(100, coefs[,1]*new.x[1] + coefs[,2] *new.x[2],ses[1])
y2.pred <- rnorm(100, coefs[,3]*y1.pred + coefs[,4] *new.x[2], ses[2])

#get some properties
mean(y2.pred)
sd(y2.pred)

At the beginning of this thread, I suggested to use predict(), with a
newdata argument. Unfortunately, it turned out that the newdata argument
for the predict() function in lavaan was not even implemented. An
oversight on my part, which is now fixed, and the dev version (0.5-10)
now has a newdata argument. You can install the dev version by typing in R:

install.packages("lavaan", repos="http://www.da.ugent.be", type="source")

I also mentioned a couple of times that the predict() function in lavaan
only produces factor scores. Hence, for observed-variables-only models,
this is not very useful. On the other hand, you can always create
phantom latent variables (with a single indicator). In this case, all
the regressions are among latent variables. And, you can use predict()
to get (factor) scores.

In other words, to get your predictions, simply 'upgrade' the dependent
variables to latent variables with a single indicator, and use the
predict() function with new data.

An artificial example:

myModel <- ' # path model
                x1 ~ x2 + x3
                x3 ~ x4 + x5
                x5 ~ x6 + x8

              # upgrading endogenous variables to latents
                fx1 =~ x1
                fx3 =~ x3
                fx5 =~ x5
            '

fit <- sem(model=myModel, data=HolzingerSwineford1939)
predict(fit)

# create new dataset - should contain the same variable names as original
HS20 <- HolzingerSwineford1939[1:20,]

predict(fit, newdata=HS20)

Yves.

messages.body_plain:
On 10/27/2012 01:44 PM, Dr. Hans Hansen wrote:
>
> Thanks, Yves!
>
> I thought, regression analysis in a sem framework would make a lot of
> sense to handle missing values when one could estimate parameters with
> fiml. Generally, would you agree on that and do you plan to implement
> that im lavaan?

I do plan to implement vanilla ML estimation (with either probit or
logit link) as an alternative to WLS(MV) in the near future.

And yes, fiml is technically perfectly possible. However, you should
make a distinction between the dependent variable(s), and the
(exogenous) independent variables. If we consider all variables as
random (and assume multivariate normality) we can use fiml (this
corresponds with fixed.x=FALSE). But if we treat the independent
variables as fixed (fixed.x=TRUE), which is the classic regression
approach, all observations with missing values on those exogenous
variables should be deleted first.

lavaan currently (0.5) does NOT make this distinction. It happily
ignores the fixed.x=TRUE flag when missing="ml" is requested. This is
not bad per se, unless you have dummy/binary predictors. Still, in 0.6,
lavaan _will_ respect the fixed.x flag when using the fiml estimator
(and hence, by default, delete all cases with missing values on those
'fixed x' predictors, unless the user explicitly specifies fixed.x=FALSE)

Yves.

imp <- mice(temp,m=5,print=F)

imputedData <- NULL
for(i in 1:5) {

Hi Ya,

The imp$imputations is not the way to get imputed data. The complete function, instead, is used to get the imputed data in mice. See the following code for an example:

model.syntax <- '
  # intercept and slope with fixed coefficients
    i =~ 1*t1 + 1*t2 + 1*t3 + 1*t4
    s =~ 0*t1 + 1*t2 + 2*t3 + 3*t4

  # regressions
    i ~ x1 + x2
    s ~ x1 + x2
'

# Note: This is used to impose missing data in the Demo.growth data
library(simsem)
temp <- Demo.growth
temp[,paste0("t", 1:4)] <- imposeMissing(temp[,paste0("t", 1:4)], pmMCAR=0.2)

imp <- mice(temp,m=5,print=F)

imputedData <- NULL
for(i in 1:5) {
imputedData[[i]] <- complete(x=imp, action=i, include=FALSE)
}

out <- runMI(model.syntax, data=imputedData, fun="growth")
